set.title: Improper fractions & mixed numbers · Unit Test

questions.question: Three identical fraction bars are drawn side by side. Each bar is cut into 4 equal parts. The first two bars are shaded completely, and 3 of the 4 parts in the third bar are shaded. Which improper fraction tells how much is shaded?
questions.explain: One whole is ONE bar, so count the shaded quarters: 4 + 4 + 3 = 11 quarters, which is 11/4. The usual trap is 11/12 — that counts all 12 parts of the three bars as if the three bars together were one whole.

questions.question: Write 3 2/5 as an improper fraction.
questions.explain: Each whole is 5 fifths, so 3 wholes = 3 × 5 = 15 fifths, and adding the extra 2 fifths gives 17/5. The most common slip is stopping at 15/5 and forgetting to add the numerator 2.

questions.question: Write 23/6 as a mixed number.
questions.explain: Divide: 23 ÷ 6 = 3 remainder 5, so there are 3 whole ones and 5 sixths left over, giving 3 5/6. Watch out for swapping the quotient and the remainder (5 3/6) — the denominator 6 never changes, because the pieces are still sixths.

questions.question: A number line shows the whole numbers 3, 4 and 5, and the space between each pair of whole numbers is divided into 3 equal parts. Aria puts her dot on the second tick mark after 3. Which improper fraction names Aria's dot?
questions.explain: The dot is 3 wholes plus 2 thirds, and 3 wholes = 9/3, so 9/3 + 2/3 = 11/3. Two common traps: writing only 2/3 (ignoring the 3 whole units) or losing one whole and writing 8/3.

questions.question: At recess in Surrey, four friends measured their skipping ropes. Ben's rope is 1 1/2 m, Chloe's is 1 5/8 m, Dev's is 1 3/8 m and Ava's is 7/4 m. Whose rope is the longest?
questions.explain: Rename every length in eighths: Ben 12/8, Chloe 13/8, Dev 11/8, Ava 7/4 = 14/8, so Ava's rope is longest. The trap is judging by how the numbers look — many students pick 1 5/8 because 5/8 is the biggest fraction on the page, or skip 7/4 because it is not written as a mixed number.

questions.question: At a Grade 6 pizza party in Kelowna, every pizza is cut into 6 equal slices. At the end of the party there are 3 5/6 pizzas left over. How many slices are left?
questions.explain: Each whole pizza is 6 slices, so 3 × 6 = 18 slices, plus the 5 extra slices = 23 slices, which is 23/6 of a pizza. Answering 18 means forgetting the 5 loose slices, and answering 8 means adding 3 + 5 instead of multiplying by the denominator first.

questions.question: On a beach walk near Tofino, Mateo's group measured four pieces of driftwood: piece A is 11/5 m, piece B is 2 1/4 m, piece C is 230 cm, and piece D is 2 1/10 m. Which piece is the longest?
questions.explain: First change 230 cm into metres: 230 cm = 2 3/10 m. Then rename everything in twentieths: A = 2 4/20, B = 2 5/20, C = 2 6/20, D = 2 2/20, so piece C is longest. The big trap is skipping the cm to m conversion; the second trap is choosing 11/5 just because 11 is the largest number written down.

questions.question: Priya is packing granola bars for a camping trip on Vancouver Island. Each box holds exactly 8 bars. She fills 3 boxes and has 5 loose bars, and then her cousin gives her 6 more loose bars. Written as a mixed number of boxes, with the fraction part less than one whole box, how many boxes does Priya have?
questions.explain: There are now 5 + 6 = 11 loose bars, and 11 bars = one full box of 8 with 3 bars left, so 3 + 1 = 4 boxes and 3/8 of a box: 4 3/8. The classic mistake is leaving the answer as 3 11/8 — the same amount, but not regrouped, and a mixed number must have a fraction part smaller than one whole; forgetting to count that new fourth box gives 3 3/8.
